title: Adam Smith's Pin Factory and the Economics of Specialization (1776)
explainer: In 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776), Adam Smith used a small pin-making workshop to argue that splitting one job into many narrow, repeated tasks let ten workers turn out tens of thousands of pins a day — far more than the same workers could produce independently. His three reasons — greater dexterity from repetition, time saved by not switching tasks, and new tools invented around a narrow task — are the same tradeoffs a self-taught engineer weighs when deciding whether to specialize in one niche or stay a generalist. It is the foundational statement of why narrowing scope can multiply output, for pin-makers and programmers alike.
